To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) TGF‐β inhibits hepatocyte proliferation in vivo and in vitro, (b) hepatocellular carcinoma cells are resistant to TGF‐β‐induced growth inhibition and apoptosis, (c) resistance to TGF‐beta‐induced growth arrest and apoptosis in HCC is caused by a loss of TGFβ‐receptor signaling, and (d) TGF‐beta is involved in the regulation of angiogenesis in HCC.
TGF‐β has a role as growth inhibitor in the normal liver.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
TGF‐β appears to be a major growth‐regulatory factor in the liver.
TGF‐β may have a tumor suppressor function in the early phase of hepatocarcinogenensis, but may have a tumor promoter function in the late phase of hepatocellular tumor development.
TGF‐β has an important role in hepatocarcino‐genesis.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
TGF‐β may be a double‐edged sword in the liver, i.e., a factor that is required to control liver growth, but may also be involved in hepatocarcinal development.
TGF‐β plays an important role as a negative growth regulator in the liver and that its role as a tumor suppressor gene is not restricted to the liver but is also valid for other organs.
TGF‐β has an important role in the control of liver growth, but its function is complex and may vary with the cell type and the microenvironment.
